body:
- **Defence is the cleanest "policy → rerating" case.** In the early phase, multiples doubled before earnings caught up. That means future returns depend on order-book execution, which explains why 2025–26 coverage shows the sector diverging (HAL/BEL holding up while shipbuilders depend on subsidy support — [Whalesbook](https://www.whalesbook.com/news/English/aerospace-defense/Defence-Stocks-Diverge-HAL-BEL-Lead-as-Shipbuilders-Eye-Subsidized-Growth/69942e9acffb93b3e927e0b7)).
- The Deepak Nitrite and Eicher arcs show that the *exit* matters. Both peaked and then derated or consolidated for years (Eicher's 2018–2020 slump is **[UNVERIFIED]**), so multibaggers often give back part of their gains.
- Cases not researched with sources this session: Bajaj Finance, Page, Astral, Tata Elxsi, railway PSUs, Polycab, Avanti Feeds, Netflix, Tesla, Apple, Super Micro and Palantir. All are well-known multibaggers, but treat any numbers for them as unverified until sourced.

**Replicable**
- Buying quality during pessimism and holding through a full cycle.
- Separating trading and investing books.
- Judging promoter character.
- Cost discipline as a business moat (D-Mart).
- Sizing up with conviction as a thesis proves out.

**Circumstance and timing**
- Entering in the mid-1980s, before liberalisation (1991) and a roughly 500x Sensex rise.
- A thin, inefficient market with lax rules.

**Network**
- Broker family (Damani), client money (Jhunjhunwala), and cartel or market-operator circles (folklore).

**Luck and survivorship**
- The 1992 shorts nearly failed before the scam broke (Damani folklore).
- Titan's outcome depended on the Tata group and the formalisation of jewellery, which was not knowable in 2002.
- Many leveraged bears and bulls of that era went bust and are not profiled.
- Leverage when young worked for these two, but it is the same tool that destroyed peers.

**How retail F&O traders fare (SEBI studies)**
- About 91% of individual traders made net losses in equity derivatives in FY25, a similar share to FY24. Net losses were ₹1,05,603 crore in FY25 vs ₹74,812 crore in FY24 (+41%). The loss share was 90.2% in FY22, 91.7% in FY23 and 91.1% in FY24 — [Business Standard, Jul 2025](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/markets/news/net-losses-of-traders-in-fo-widens-in-fy25-sebi-study-125070701221_1.html); [Moneylife](https://moneylife.in/article/91-percentage-of-retail-traders-lost-money-in-derivatives-losses-in-fo-surged-41-percentage-to-rs105-lakh-crore-in-fy25-sebi-study/77613.html)
- Unique F&O traders fell about 20% to 42.7 lakh after SEBI's curbs — [Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/markets/news/individual-investors-shrink-20-percent-fo-segment-125070800801_1.html)
- In FY24, proprietary traders made about ₹33,000 crore gross profit while individuals lost over ₹61,000 crore before costs. This figure comes from a secondary summary — [NISM blog](https://www.nism.ac.in/blog/equity-linked-exchange-traded-derivative-contracts-the-retail-rush-and-regulatory-measures/)
- The longer an individual trades F&O, the more likely they are to lose money — [Value Research](https://www.valueresearchonline.com/stories/225398/average-trader-lost-rs-1-1-lakh-fo-fy25/)

body:
`case_study:suzlon-turnaround-2020-2024` · tickers: SUZLON · confidence: verified

After falling −99.6% from 2008 (see case_study:suzlon), the price went from ₹1.70 (Mar 2020) → ₹83.5 (Sep 2024) ≈49x. P/E is not meaningful because EPS was negative until FY23; the engine was balance-sheet repair. Steps: a 2020 lender restructuring; an Oct 2022 rights issue of ₹1,200 cr at ₹5/share (1.8x subscribed, ~₹600 cr to debt); an Aug 2023 QIP that took the company to net cash of ₹599 cr (Sep 2023) from net debt of ₹1,180 cr (Mar 2023). The share count rose heavily (exact figure unverified). Most of the move came in 2023 (₹10 → ₹38). Revenue FY21 ₹3,346 cr → FY26 ₹16,732 cr; OPM 16–18%; FY26 PAT ₹3,163 cr included a ₹718 cr tax write-back. Early signal: an offer to all shareholders at ₹5 with the founder family participating, order inflows (C&I, hybrid), and the net-cash milestone, all in exchange filings. Ended/stalled: −59% to ₹33.9 (Oct 2026); Q2 FY27 PAT −69% YoY against the tax-boosted base, flat EBITDA with lower margin, the EPC share of the order book rising to 38%; order book still >6 GW. P/E ~22 now. Lesson: distressed-equity repair can 50x a near-dead stock, but once it is clean it rerates to a normal multiple and becomes an execution and margin story.

Key data: **start_year**: 2020; **end_year**: 2024; **start_price**: 1.7; **end_price**: 83.5; **price_nov2026**: 36.95; **multiple**: ~49x; **pe_start**: n/m (losses); **pe_end**: ~110-119 (2024); **eps_multiple_implied**: n/m; **max_drawdown**: -52% (2020) in run; -59% after; **early_signals**: 2022 rights at ₹5; 2023 QIP; net cash Sep 2023; **ended**: normal multiple + margin pressure 2026; **lesson**: turnarounds = equity repair, then execution

Sources: <https://www.screener.in/company/SUZLON/consolidated/> · <https://www.business-standard.com/amp/article/markets/suzlon-energy-rights-issue-subscribed-1-8-times-stock-down-3-7-122102001297_1.html> · <https://www.mercomindia.com/suzlon-net-profit-q3-debt-free> · <https://www.businesstoday.in/markets/company-stock/story/suzlon-energy-eyes-debt-reduction-of-rs-900-crore-through-rights-issue-proceeds-349510-2022-10-11> · <https://www.indiainfoline.com/news/companies/suzlon-energy-shares-fall-9-as-net-profit-declines-69-for-q2> · <https://insights.dsij.in/dsijarticledetail/suzlon-share-price-sees-sharpest-single-day-fall-in-3-months-nears-3-year-low-after-q2-results>

CFO = PAT + non-cash charges ± changes in working capital. A sudden jump in CFO can come from:
- delaying payments to suppliers (a payables stretch)
- selling receivables (factoring)
- collecting customer advances

All three reverse later. **Test:** split CFO into (a) CFO before working-capital changes and (b) the working-capital change. If (b) supplies more than about 30% of CFO two years running, ask which line moved and whether it can repeat.

1. The total cash lease cost is principal ₹320 cr + interest ₹150 cr = ₹470 cr, which approximates the straight-line operating-lease expense. Comparable EBITDA ≈ 1,000 − 470 = **₹530 cr**. Lease depreciation and interest are already below EBITDA, so subtract the rent equivalent once.
2. Benign: (a) timing, since bank statements were prepared before quarter-end adjustments; (b) valuation basis, with statements at selling price and books at cost. Malign: (a) inflating drawing power to borrow more; (b) inventory in the books later written down, i.e. phantom stock. Follow-up: read the reconciliation the company must give in its notes, check whether the gap persists in Q4, and compare inventory days against peers.
3. **3(ix)** defaults/fund diversion → **3(xi)** fraud → **3(xviii)** auditor resignation → **3(iii)** related-party loans → **3(xix)** liquidity uncertainty. These five map to the disqualifiers in `insight:forensic-redflag-checklist`: diversion, fraud, auditor exit, related-party leakage, and survival.
